column5: Lord’s mercy trains and turns back like a shepherd
column6: Sirach describes the Lord’s compassion as rebuking, training, teaching, and turning creatures back as a shepherd turns his flock; it gathers the commentary’s merciful rab, tamed animal, straying, and restoration into one Jewish formulation.

column5: donkey turns aside because it sees the angel
column6: Balaam’s donkey leaves the road after seeing the divine messenger while its human rider cannot see and beats it. The scene reverses the surface value of an animal’s turning aside: the animal is the one properly guided, sharpening the commentary’s animal-and-human contrast.

column5: trained heifer; fair neck; harness
column6: Hosea calls Ephraim a trained heifer and describes placing a yoke on its fair neck for work; this is a close prophetic animal image for the commentary’s muʿabbad camel and its guiding neck.

column5: cords of love; yoke lifted; feeding
column6: God leads Israel with cords of kindness and love, lifts the yoke from its jaws, and bends down to feed it. The verse combines animal training, gentle leading, pasture-like provision, and divine compassion.

column5: wild ox will not serve or stay at the manger
column6: The divine questions ask whether the wild ox will consent to serve a human or spend the night at the manger, directly contrasting a human-owned, tamed herd with a wild bovine beyond ordinary possession.

column5: wild ox bound to furrow and harrow
column6: The next question tests whether the wild ox can be bound with a cord to plow and harrow; it supplies the laboring, guided-animal side of the commentary’s mount carried and directed by its body.

column5: camel humps carrying treasure through hard country
column6: The oracle pictures wealth carried on camels’ humps through a land of distress, a specific Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary’s animals carrying burdens to distant places.

column5: where the shepherd pastures and lets flock rest
column6: The beloved asks where the shepherd pastures his flock and makes it lie down at noon, directly matching the commentary’s owner, grazing place, and place of remaining.

column5: follow flock tracks and pasture kids near shepherd tents
column6: The reply directs the seeker to go out by the tracks of the flock and pasture her kids beside shepherds’ tents; it gives an unusually exact literary image of following a herd’s route toward a shepherded grazing place.

column5: led by water on a straight path without stumbling
column6: God promises to lead the returning people by streams of water on a straight way where they will not stumble, binding the commentary’s guidance request, straight path, and animal-water/pasture scene.

column5: compassionate guide leads to water springs
column6: The compassionate one leads the hungry and thirsty and guides them by springs of water, a direct guide-and-pasture counterpart to the hādī leading a herd.

column5: flock wanders for lack of shepherd
column6: The people wander like sheep and suffer because there is no shepherd, making the absence of the commentary’s front-leading, responsible figure the stated cause of dispersion.

column5: know the condition of flocks and attend to herds
column6: The proverb requires careful knowledge of the state of one’s flock and attention to herds, adding the sustained ownerly care absent from the unknown-owner definition of the dālla.

column5: a sheep fallen into a pit is lifted out
column6: Jesus assumes that an owner will take hold of and lift out a sheep fallen into a pit even on the Sabbath, a concrete recovery scene for the commentary’s animal left in an exposed place.

column5: found sheep carried on shoulders
column6: After finding the lost sheep, the shepherd lays it on his shoulders with joy; this supplies the bodily return of the escaped animal that the preceding search scene alone does not state.

column5: owner unties ox or donkey and leads it to water
column6: Jesus describes each person untying an ox or donkey from the stall and leading it to water, joining a known owner, a restrained domestic animal, purposeful leading, and animal provision.

column5: overseers shepherd God’s acquired flock
column6: The elders must shepherd God’s flock, which God acquired, while serving as overseers. It distinguishes the true owner from delegated guides in a way that closely illuminates the commentary’s rab/mālik and leading-animal relation.

column5: shepherd the flock of God under oversight
column6: The elders are told to shepherd the flock of God and exercise oversight, a specific Christian instruction about the responsibility attached to leading another’s flock.

column5: untrained calf asks to be turned back
column6: Ephraim compares itself to an untrained calf and asks God to turn it back. The image gives the commentary’s tamed animal and its loss of direction a penitential human counterpart.

column5: shepherd moderates pace for tender flock
column6: Jacob says tender children and nursing flocks cannot be driven hard without losing the herd. It adds a concrete criterion for a leader’s guidance: the front-moving party must accommodate the flock it leads.

column5: animals teach the human questioner
column6: Job invites the sufferer to ask the animals, which will teach him. This develops the commentary’s secondary reversal in which animal life may disclose what a human who has lost the way fails to know.

column5: wild asses drink from God’s waters
column6: God’s waters give drink to beasts of the field and quench the thirst of wild asses, giving the commentary’s ownerless wild-ass image a providential water-and-habitat setting.

column5: wild donkey wandering alone
column6: Hosea compares political wandering to a wild donkey going alone; it supplies a biblical use of the wild-ass figure for self-directed separation rather than the secure movement of a herd.

column5: called by name and declared God’s own
column6: The creator calls Israel by name and says “you are mine,” a human counterpart to the commentary’s brand that makes an animal’s belonging and owner recognizable.

column5: working ox must not be muzzled
column6: The law preserves the feeding claim of an ox while it works, adding an ethical limit to treating the commentary’s tamed, useful animal solely as a bearer of human benefit.

column5: flock-tender receives milk from the flock
column6: Paul’s labor argument asks who tends a flock without drinking its milk. Alongside his ox citation, this turns the material benefit of a tended flock into an analogy for the guide’s rightful support.

column5: seal says the Lord knows those who are his
column6: God’s firm foundation bears a seal declaring that the Lord knows those who are his, a textual counterpart to the commentary’s visible mark and the lost camel whose owner cannot be known.

column5: take my yoke and learn from me
column6: Jesus’ invitation to take his yoke and learn makes animal harness a figure for guided discipleship, offering a Christian transformation of the commentary’s subdued, neck-directed animal.
